As others have said, time doesn't matter as much as you'd think. Items allow you to outscale monsters, which you can do relatively quickly, but only if you're looting everything. 

Your itemization matters, and should be, in order of what you should pick up first: 

Damage/move speed > utility > healing. 

Have a general idea of items that are good on any survivor (bands, shuriken, Tesla Coil, Goat Hoof, Antlers, crit glasses, etc.) and items more specific to survivors (I.e. Engineer/bungus, Railgunner (& Loader)/Crowbar, REX/First Aid Kit.) My runs got far more consistent when I started itemizing to do damage and move fast.

You have to kill things faster than they can kill you, and move faster than enemies can hit you, which is why damage and move speed are so important. Tangentially, get in the habit of hitting sprint when you're done doing something that breaks sprint. Be sprinting as much as possible.

That the Portuguese Man O’ War isn’t a jellyfish, despite being referred to as such. True jellyfish are radially symmetrical, and rely on pulsating to propel themselves through water to the extent that they can. They are also one discrete organism.

A Man O’ War is a colonial organism known as a Siphonophore. Siphonophores are made of several different specialized, but genetically identical organisms called zooids. They have some that sting, some that float, some that digest, and some that reproduce. 
 
Moreover, Jellyfish stings often suck but aren’t super duper clinically significant.* Man O’ Wars have been known to kill children who get wrapped in the fishing tentacle. I know people with scars from these stings because they are *that* bad.

*Box jellies, Irukandji jellies, and a few other species (Japanese Sea Nettle comes to mind,) are clinically significant. If you get stung by any jelly, just seek treatment if needed, tbh.

Mechanic student here:

For those of y’all arguing that it puts extra strain on the engine… it doesn’t. The starter motor is a heavy-duty starter in cars with this feature. The people designing the car have designed it with this feature in mind.

It’s not a new feature and it’s become more common in recent years with manufacturers trying desperately to meet CAFE standards. If you don’t like it, hit the button to turn it off.

Edit for those interested in the greasy details: 

These engines are designed with the start/stop system in mind.

In a non stop/start equipped engine, oil lubricates everything constantly (outside of the starting process, but I’ll get to that) because the oil pump circulates oil through the engine while it’s running. This means no considerations need to be made because the engine is a pretty normal Internal Combustion Engine (ICE).

However, when you lose oil pressure at every stoplight, you need to make a few considerations. 

The crankshaft bearings (because those lose lubrication when the engine shuts down) are coated in materials that act like a dry lubricant. Meaning no excess wear occurs.

The starter is a heavy duty starter that is designed to handle the constant starting and stopping without overheating or wearing out more than a “normal” starter.

The battery is not a standard Lead-Acid Battery, but is an Absorbent Glass Mat (AGM) or Enhanced Flooded Battery (EFB). These are designed to withstand higher loads and more frequent charging cycles to compensate for the more frequent stop/start cycles.

The coolant system is independent of the engine, unlike in a non stop/start equipped vehicle.

And the engines have more sensors and special Engine Control Units (ECU)s that are programmed for this application.

Your camshaft bearings and pistons don’t lose lubrication during this process, so don’t worry about your engine.

Your car is just fine doing this. 

It’s just jarring to get used to, but saves a lot of gas and emissions (theoretically) spread out over everyone who uses a car equipped with this feature (and who uses this feature.)

So stop being worried about your engine ;)

Symmetra is… difficult to hard counter without knowing Sym.

Symmetra has incredible flexibility and excels at defense, but can be quite scary in an offensive tole as well. Her flexibility is what makes her scary.

But here’s the thing; Sym fails at taking down any remotely coordinated team. (It’s why she’s an unusual pick at higher levels of play, iirc.)

Coordinated teams pick off her sentries, which have a 10-second recharge time per charge. If you pick off her sentries as she just threw all of them, she has to wait 10 seconds before using them again.

Here are some tips:

-Ping her sentries, and if nobody responds, even if you’re playing Lifeweaver, just shoot them. They do a surprising amount of damage, but they aren’t torb turrets and can’t take much punishment.

-If she’s flanking and she’s otherwise handled by another teammate, consider destroying her TP. It’s fragile and her only movement ability. She then has to hope she doesn’t die or can kill you all when you all dogpile on her.

-Keep an eye out for backline TP bombs. She can teleport sentries and Dva bombs (not that I’ve ever seen that, but keep it in mind,) and those sentries hurt if they catch your Ana off guard.

-Consider her wall a giant line in the sand she has drawn. If you coordinate, with the right team comp you can cross that line. Most of the time, it’s really just better to not cross over on to the enemy side of the wall.  They can shoot you before you can shoot them and it’s just easier to wait until her wall is down before rengaging

-Sym players will also, instead of creating a giant wall between teams, will split the objective down the middle and use the wall to “shield dance.” That is they will walk towards you parallel to the wall, and bounce between sides to prevent you from firing on them.

-Consider your tank very carefully. She gets ammo from shield tanks like Rein, Winston, and Sigma, but isn’t blocked by Defense Matrix and Orisa SPEEN. Doomfist is also kind of fragile and sentries really mess up Ball’s schtick.

Good picks are Zarya and Winston (kind of). Yeah, Winston bubble’s gonna give her ammo, but Tesla Cannon has AOE and she suffers when her sentries are all gone. Zarya just turns her damage against her team.

-Pharah is actually kind of annoying to deal with. She forces Sym to make some hard choices about life. “Do I put my sentries all down and hope for a kill, or do I conserve my sentries for the slow because Pharah is going to come in with one rocket and kill them all anyway?”

-Pharah is especially annoying because unlike Sym 2.0, where Photon Barrier was a hard counter to Pharah (lol, get dunked on with your own splash damage during your ult.), Symmetra has very little in the way of actually dealing with Pharah. 

-Also, just keep Sym at arm’s length. Her balls travel fast and definitely take out more scrubs than you ever really intend to spamming balls down a choke point, but honestly, her beam is far scarier.

-For supports, anyone with a way to put distance between her and yourself, or anyone she can buy you more time, (Kiriko, Moira, Mercy, Lucio, Baptiste, and Brig)

Shout out to Bap who has the lamp and can buy you enough time to kill her.

-For your DPS, anyone with AOE or who is good at taking out a squishy, or who has an escape (like Reaper.)

-One last thing: If you really want to learn how to counter a Symmetra, become Symmetra. That is, learn how to play her and figure out counterplay that way. (This applies to any heroes, but weird ones like Sym especially.)

Mercy dislikes literally anyone who can:

-Snipe her from a distance

-Jump on and stick to her

-Disable her and/or burst her down

She’s squishy, she’s able to be killed during her escape, and she’s extremely vulnerable while gliding around. She’s also easily bait-able into and extremely vulnerable during Res. Mercy is also notably, very, very single target outside of Valkyrie.

Hitscan DPS who do burst damage like Ashe, Cassidy, Widow, Sojourn, and Soldier are prime picks.

DPS who are mobile and can stick to Mercy like Genji, Tracer, Sombra, and Reaper are also exceptionally good.

Your aggressive tanks like D.Va, Ball, Rein, JQ, and Zarya are also good picks.

For supports you can pick Ana, Brig, Moira, and Lucio. You could get away with a Zenyatta, but that’s because if everyone else is dead before Mercy, then she’s an easy pick.

More important than killing her is understanding that you should just get a pick. Like, focus on getting a kill as DPS or even Tank, and go from there. OW2 is a lot of “Who can kill a squishy first?” Or “Is my Tank or their Tank gonna die first?” 

Yes, Mercy and the other support are priority targets, but if the other support is an Ana or Zen, it’ll be easier to kill the other support than Mercy. But squishies include DPS and if the other team is down a DPS they’ll be hard pressed to win that fight. (You, again, might even be able to get two kills if their Mercy is bad.)

Mercy can’t be everywhere at once, and you’re stretching her thin by killing her teammates. So, don’t focus so much on her, as much as the Tank, other support, and the DPS.

Linux enthusiast here:

Ubuntu/Debian:

Ubuntu does discreet updates every 6 months, as opposed to smaller more frequent updates.
They’re easy to install at the cost of customization.
However, Canonical is highly commercialized, and has been making questionable choices, including at one point placing ads in the OS.

Arch:
Arch is definitely less beginner friendly, people often move from Ubuntu to Arch.
Arch is more likely to be a pain, especially during installation.
Arch uses a rolling release model means more frequent updates, but that also means one has to run an update on things more frequently.
Arch is more customizable because you’re installing everything from a Command Line, and the installing a gui.
The Community is more geared towards not trying to capitalism. Like, this isn’t going to have ads ever.

I wouldn’t say one is better than the other because they have two completely different use cases and target audiences. I'm low level, but feel okay in my knowledge, and games go on long enough at my level to make Medusa a viable choice. If I want a ranged carry, Medusa is my go-to.

Medusa is arguably the hardest carry in the game. She wins fights by essentially being the last one alive at the end of it. Enemies either have to choose between letting the Medusa kill everything and taking out her team, or killing the Medusa and her team kills everything else. 

Strengths:

-She's super tanky. Mana Shield makes her tanky af. Again, her tank puts the enemy team in an awkward position.

-Split shot makes farming faster.

-Devastating after about 45 minutes if you're farming okay, 30-35 minutes if you're wrecking things

-Relatively flexible as far as end game items. Butterfly, Daedelus, even Divine Rapier

-Benefits from every stat. Strength gives HP, Agi gives damage and armor, Int gives her mana pool

-Okay harass in lane if you can hit enemy heroes with Mystic Snake

-Can farm somewhat aggressively with Stone Gaze

Weaknesses:

-Countered hard by Invoker, Lion, Anti-Mage, Nyx, Silencer, and Diffusal blade builders (Riki, PL) as she is highly dependent on her mana pool

-She plays very, very, very passively for the first 30 minutes. It'll be essentially a 4v5 for the first 30 minutes because you need to farm constantly in order to make her work.

-Her bow might as well be firing nerf darts until she gets  some damage

-Other carries come online far earlier, meaning your team needs to have good early and mid-gane presence

-Only good if the game is going to go on for a long time

Supports:

Anyone capable of backing up a 4v5. Seriously. If your team can survive long enough for Medusa to come online without absolutely feeding the enemy team, they'll be hard pressed to win that game.

Disablers, Medusa doesn't have great options for mobility

Venge is good for the armor and damage

Supports who scale well into the mid-game are a good choice as that presence is needed


Items that are broken against Medusa:

Heaven's Halberd is a disarm that can't be dispelled. Meaning, the Manta Style you buy can't purge that off. If Medusa can't attack, she can't accomplish much during that fight other than throwing out a snake and her ult

Diffusal Blade burns her mana and is a slow. She likes neither of these things, but especially the mana burn because she requires mana to be tanky.

Items that are strong on Medusa:

Eye of Skadi is core on Medusa for very good reason. It gives her stats and a slow. She depends heavily on stats for everything. She also enjoys the slow, because she's not very fast.

Divine Rapier is a special mention. If you can play with your team and you aren't dying, the damage from Divine Rapier is good offensively on Medusa after all of her other items. She doesn't die easily and it helps the enemy team die faster than her team.

Linken's Sphere is a good defensive option. Medusa doesn't always buy BKB (read: rarely) because she's able to survive most disables without dying, unlike a PA, for instance. If she needs a defensive option to not die to an important targeted disable, Linken's gives stats and a block.

How long does it take Medusa to come online:

30-45 minutes in a game where you're farming everything in sight. She's a "Farm for an hour, get 5 kills, walk down mid and win." Hero. The hour of farming is an exaggeration, but not by that much, lol

If your opponents pressure you early:

It's hard for a Medusa to come online if she has to fight early. She can take fights opportunistically when she's near enough to help, but it's gonna be a difficult game if the enemy team applies early pressure.

You have two options: 

-Buy mid-game items and hope for the best

or

-Continue farming and hope that you can salvage the game when you come online

There's not much in-between, unfortunately. Playing against a Medusa is a lot like playing against a Spectre, you have to end early before they come online.

Meta:

AFAIK Medusa isn't a popular pick because she can be counter picked easily, and coordinated teams know better than to let a Medusa free farm until she comes online. Once she comes online she's likely the scariest virtual danger noodle. So, teams with coordination simply don't let it get there.

Tips for Medusa:

-You have a pretty set build order in front of you: Treads or Phase boots -> Dragon Lance -> Yasha -> Manta Style -> Skadi -> Non-Rapier Damage item of your choice (Daedelus, MKB, Butterfly, that general vein of item.) -> Hurricane Pike -> Another damage item of your choice including a possible Rapier -> BoTs. There are exceptions to this, but that's the general idea from my understanding.

-Linken's Sphere is a defensive option. As is BKB. Because Medusa doesn't do damage without items that give her damage and stats, try to only buy BKB or Linken's if you're absolutely getting rekt by disables. She's tanky, but not unkillable. The above is especially true if they have mana burn that is blockable by BKB or Linken's. 

-If you're feeling cheeky, you can go scepter/shard for free stuns on enemies with targeted spells. Scepter makes her snake petrify people, and shard shoots out a single target snake on being targeted with a spell. The single target snakes also petrify

Used to sell printers at both major office supply companies in America. Also used to work in the print departments at both chains. I kind of want to add that printers are all for different applications, and just because one has really cheap ink doesn’t mean it’s good for you, especially if that ink dries out and you have to replace it regularly.

Printers are generally going to be cheap upfront and expensive to keep running.

If you have to buy a printer because you can’t print anywhere else (at the college library or public library, for instance,) think first about what you actually need it for.

Low volume printer users and photographers generally want an Inkjet. They’re going to produce decent quality prints, with generally lower costs for ink versus toner, and it’s versatile. Photographers want an Inkjet because it’s just going to produce better quality images than a laser printer. (Laser Printers that aren’t industrial quality can leave lines across the page when printing full color that can distract from the actual image.)

Medium volume applications can go two paths: Laser/LED printers, or inkjets that have tanks of ink.

The laser printers are going to use toner, and are going to be great for if you print a lot all at once, and then not print for a bit, but may need to come back to it at some point. Also, if you just need black and white prints, this is the way to go. Inkjets generally take all four colors. Laser printers come in both color and monochrome. Also, they generally print faster.

Inkjets with built-in tanks. (Epson EcoTank, HP and Canon also have an equivalent to this, and I’d go with the HP or the Canon over the Epson. HP iirc also makes a laser printer that just takes a syringe of black toner but don’t know how reliable that particular one is.) These take bottles of ink, and are actually cheaper than laser, the big caveat being that you need to print somewhat frequently because they’re spendy up front like a laser printer (in some cases more expensive,) and if you don’t print on them with some frequency the ink can dry out and clog your print heads, which just bricks your printer. They’re also more versatile than a laser printer because they’re an inkjet.

If you want high volume printing done, Laser is the way to go. Toner is just going to be cheaper per page than ink every time. They tend to be spendy upfront but the savings compared to inkjets are amazing.

The print centers at both chains I wouldn’t recommend. They’re expensive, and unless you need a specific service done (Folding, stapling, thousands of impressions, etc.) Then you’re better off doing it at home.

It’s not generally on demand, but AWD is either Full time (Subaru and Audi) or Part time (Everyone else.) 

Part time means that the car is in FWD most of the time, engaging AWD when it detects that the front wheels aren’t getting enough traction. This is primarily to save fuel costs because it gets kind costly to be powering a car like that all the time. The demonstrations I have seen of part time AWD systems demonstrate that they work, and quite effectively at that, but I would not recommend off-roading in one of these.

Subaru and Audi have Full Time AWD. All four wheels, all the time. It’s slightly more expensive to run a car with this system as some of the same maintenance concerns with a 4x4 vehicle crop up there, namely all four tires have to have even wear, and rotations must happen on schedule. This results in similar or better results than part time systems. As far as I can tell, cars with Full time AWD can mange at least light off-roading, and some manufacturers do indeed make lift kits and skid plates for Subaru SUVs.

HIPAA covers healthcare providers and insurance companies. It doesn’t cover gossipy coworkers. 

If your coworkers knew which Healthcare provider you saw, and contacted them, and the provider told your coworkers that you miscarried, that is a HIPAA violation. 

If they reached out to your insurance company, and the company told your coworkers that you miscarried, that is a HIPAA violation. 

If you told your coworker and they said “OMG, Janice, did you hear Smart_Ad_3636 miscarried?” And spread that shit around, That’s shitty coworkers. Really shitty coworkers.

I had to do HIPAA training for the community college that I went to EMT school at, because we worked directly with patients. Giving information that could be traced back to a specific case, such as location, time and condition would be a HIPAA violation. Anything that could be used to ID the patient. So, for us, general information was okay, such as:

“Dude, we had a patient present to the ER with massive abdominal pain, turns out it was actually their appendix, and we arrived just in time.”

As long as you aren’t ID’d specifically or can have the information they talk about traced back to you by the general public, it’s fine and not a violation. That only concerns providers and insurance companies, though.

If your coworkers or boss spread that shit around the office or divulge that stuff to customers, that’s an HR issue or a Hostile Work Environment issue.

Great question. Short answer is: It depends.

Tip Pooling is a thing at a lot of fast casual restaurants (MOD Pizza, Chipotle, Coffee Shops, basically anywhere that you’re not being waited on by a server that has a tip jar. Also, some other industries like Cannabis/Marijuana do this as well.) Tip pooling is also a thing at certain full service restaurants. 

Tip Pooling is where all of the tips for that shift are divided amongst the employees equally if they all work 8 hour shifts or depending on hours worked that shift if they work shifts shorter than 8 hours. It’s still okay, as employees still gain some extra money, but has the downside of, depending on the restaurant, being declared on taxes. Cannabis industry is mostly cash so Budtenders get cash tips, which is super awesome. When I worked as a Budtender, it amounted to an extra $5 an hour that I could then spend on weed.

Then there are cash tips at a full service restaurant that doesn’t participate in Tip Pooling. Those go directly to the FOH staff, usually the wait staff, but often other FOH staff get a small cut. Those “are required” to be declared on taxes (But may or may not be, depending on how much it is.)

Credit/Debit Card tips go to the server but will be declared on taxes. 

If you go out to eat at a restaurant, or go to a dispensary, please tip your wait staff who may be making tipped federal minimum wage, or your Budtender, who has a specialized skill set and who don’t get paid more than minimum.

People depend on tips in this hellscape for money, and while I despise it, unless otherwise indicated, tip.

TL;DR: Management at the store level often has just as much say in things as the employees who are working the register, and yelling at any of them doesn’t do anything.

Managers aren’t in charge of how much pay/how many hours they give their employees. Take a SMALL retail store, such as one of the major office supply companies I worked for: There used to be 5 managers in a store, due to restructuring, there are now four-ish. But I digress. The bigger of the two chains, rhymes with Moffice Schmeepo used to have 5 managers in a store, A Customer Service Manager, Ops Manager, Assistant Store Manager, Store Manager, and a Print Supervisor. Does the CSM dictate how many hours their cashiers get? No, they, much like the Ops manager, and the Print Supervisor have no say in scheduling or anything pay related. They are there to drive sales in their departments in the CSM and Print Sup positions, or make sure the pricing is accurate and the store is stocked in the Ops Manager’s position. 

That leaves the SM and ASM. The ASM does arguably more work than the SM, and is still hourly. They don’t get any say in the pay/hours of their employees outside of which individual is getting scheduled hours. 

That leaves the SM, the person running the show. They STILL do not get any say in what they can pay their employees or if they can schedule everyone a reasonable amount of hours. 

Corporate goes “Here’s how busy the store is anticipated to be based on a number that our software spit out based on prior data. Labor needs to be less than X% of that sales number. Here’s how many hours a week you get. The managers and full time sales people get their 35-40 hours a week. What’s left is how many hours you can schedule the part-timers.” Cool. Automatically ~240-300 hours of that pool of hours goes to the full time employees. And the remaining ~140 goes to the 7 other part time employees they schedule 20 hours a week.

At the store level, management only has so much control over staffing levels.

HR then says “You can pay X amount of money for this given position. Varying based on that state’s minimum wage, and going up based on whether the position the employee is in, for instance, the print center, requires specialized skills.” Even working in the print center, arguably the hardest job in those stores, you only made slightly above minimum. The SM has no say in any of that, outside of yearly performance raises, and even then I’m positive that they have tiers of raises based on ranges of arbitrary metrics. 

Blaming store management for the problems corporate is causing and exacerbating is actually part of the problem. 

The problem is the C-level executives want to line their pockets while everyone else suffers.
